extracted.intended_audience: zoologists, taxonomists, museum curators, and naturalists working on freshwater sponges, hydroids, and polyzoa (India and adjacent regions).
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for delimiting species, subspecies, varieties, phases; rules and practical conventions for designation of type specimens; and nomenclatural practice and standards to follow when describing freshwater sponges, hydroids, and polyzoa (with emphasis on Indian material).

rubrics_metrics.name: Species (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: “A group of individuals differing in constant characters of a definite nature and of systematic importance from all others in the same genus.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat this definition as the working meaning of 'species' for the volume; what counts as a character of 'systematic importance' may vary among groups (footnote: 'What characters are of systematic importance?' requires different answers for different groups). Use constant, definite characters to delimit species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subspecies (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: “An isolated or local race, the individuals of which differ from others included in the same species in characters that are constant but either somewhat indefinite or else of little systematic importance.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve 'subspecies' for geographically or reproductively isolated local races showing constant, though possibly slight or indefinite, differences of lesser systematic importance than species-level differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: “A group of individuals not isolated geographically from others of the same species but nevertheless exhibiting slight, not altogether constant, or indefinite differences from the typical form of the species (i. e. the form first described).”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'variety' for non-geographically-isolated forms with slight or inconsistent differences from the species' typical form; variety does not imply distinct geographic isolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phase (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: “A peculiar form assumed by the individuals of a species which are exposed to peculiarities in environment and differ from normal individuals as a direct result.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply 'phase' to environmentally induced morphs that differ from the typical individuals as a direct response to external conditions rather than heritable taxonomic differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference when unsure between variety and subspecies
rubrics_metrics.description: “There are cases in which imperfection of information renders it difficult or impossible to distinguish between a variety and a subspecies. In such cases it is best to call the form a variety, for this term does not imply any special knowledge as regards its distribution or the conditions in which it is found.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If data are insufficient to choose between 'variety' and 'subspecies', favour the more conservative label 'variety' because it does not assert geographic isolation or specific distributional knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the term 'form'
rubrics_metrics.description: “I use the term 'form' in a general sense of which the meaning or meanings are clear without explanation.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The generic label 'form' may be used flexibly where context makes the intended sense clear; no strict technical definition is imposed here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type specimen designation — schools of practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Two schools exist: (a) those who assert that one specimen and one only must be the type of a species, and (b) those who are willing to accept several specimens as types (paratypes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes theoretical objections to a single ideal type but acknowledges museum practice favouring a single definite type. Practically, when museum rules prevent treating the entire series as the type, select 'one specimen that seems particularly characteristic' as the type and term the remainder co-types (or paratypes). Be explicit about which specimen is chosen and why.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type designation for compound or easily divisible organisms
rubrics_metrics.description: For sponges, hydroids, and similar compound or fragment-prone specimens, selecting a single piece as the type is problematic because specimens may be compound or divisible into equivalent fragments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the practical problem: if material is broken into pieces (e.g., dried sponges), the biggest piece may be called the type and smaller pieces designated 'schizotype.' Where colonies or multi-individual specimens occur (e.g., a particular polyp in a hydroid colony), note the difficulty and be explicit about the part designated as type. Use co-types/paratypes where appropriate and document which fragments correspond to the original description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedy when multiple species are confounded as types
rubrics_metrics.description: “The difficulty as regards the confounding of specimens of two or more species as the types of one can always be adjusted if the author who discovers the mistake redescribes one of the species under the original name and regards the specimen that agrees with his description as the type, at the same time describing a new species with another of the specimens as its type.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If it is discovered that the original 'type series' includes more than one species, redescribe and reassign names: retain the original name for the specimen matching the original description (designated as the type) and describe the other distinct specimen(s) as new species with new type designations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of nomenclatural standard works
rubrics_metrics.description: The author adopts particular monographs as practical standards: e.g., for Spongillidæ no monograph earlier than Potts's 'Fresh-Water Sponges' (1887) is acceptable; freshwater polyzoa follow Allman's 'Fresh-Water Polyzoa' (1856); other polyzoa divisions follow Hincks's 'British Marine Polyzoa' (1880).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use recent comprehensive monographs as the working basis for nomenclature and avoid exhaustive synonymies of literature prior to these chosen standards. The rationale: many earlier descriptions were general, many types are lost, and detailed pursuit of obsolete names is often a waste of time. Explicitly state which authority is being followed for each group and mark non-local works with a notation (see notation conventions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of obsolete names and nomenclatural conservatism
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference to the 1908 committee protest against unearthing obsolete zoological names and the difficulty of adopting a single standard of nomenclature for entire groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise conservatism: avoid reviving obsolete names unless there is compelling reason. Prefer to follow established comprehensive treatments for the group rather than reexamining every earlier name; where disagreement exists, explain the chosen course and the authority followed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentation of examined material and repository notation
rubrics_metrics.description: “The descriptions in this volume are based on specimens in the collection of the Indian Museum... specimens from other collections have not been ignored... Our collection now includes specimens of all the Indian forms, named in nearly all cases by the author of the species, except in those of species described long ago of which no authentic original specimens can now be traced.” The following list shows where the types ... are preserved. I have included in this list the names of all species that have been found in stagnant water, whether fresh or brackish, but those of species not yet found in fresh water are enclosed in square brackets.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When publishing descriptions: base descriptions on museum-held material where possible; acknowledge specimens loaned or gifted by other institutions and individuals; provide a clear list of the repositories holding the types and the material examined. Use square brackets to mark species not yet found in fresh water; mark works not locally available with an asterisk. Be explicit about type status (type, co-type, schizotype, schizotype, 'not in existence', etc.) in the specimen table.
